scenes.headline: Environment Variables & Config
scenes.subtitle: Keeping secrets and settings out of code
scenes.narration: Hardcoded credentials are a security incident waiting to happen, which is why configuration and secrets belong in the environment rather than committed alongside your source code.

scenes.headline: Why externalize config
items: Same code across dev, staging, prod
scenes.narration: Externalizing config means one build artifact runs unchanged across development, staging, and production, with only the environment differing. It keeps passwords and API keys out of version control, where a single leaked commit can compromise everything. It also lets operators tune behavior without a redeploy. This is the essence of the twelve-factor app methodology that underpins modern deployment.

scenes.headline: Reading env vars safely
scenes.code:
import os

DB_HOST = os.environ['DB_HOST']          # required
PORT = int(os.getenv('PORT', '5432'))    # default
DEBUG = os.getenv('DEBUG', '').lower() == 'true'
scenes.narration: Bracket access on os.environ demands a value and raises immediately if DB_HOST is missing, which is exactly the fail-fast behavior you want for critical settings. For optional values, getenv accepts a default, and here we convert the port to an integer because environment variables always arrive as strings. The DEBUG line shows the common pattern of interpreting a string flag as a boolean.

scenes.headline: Loading a .env file
scenes.code:
from dotenv import load_dotenv
import os

load_dotenv()  # reads .env into os.environ
api_key = os.environ['API_KEY']
scenes.narration: The python-dotenv library reads a local .env file and loads its values into os.environ, giving you a convenient way to manage settings during development. In production, the real environment injects those variables directly, so the same os.environ lookups keep working without any code change.

scenes.text: Never commit .env or secrets; require critical vars up front so misconfig fails loudly at startup.
scenes.narration: Add .env to your gitignore so secrets never leak, and validate critical variables at startup so a misconfiguration fails loudly rather than deep inside a running job.
